fields.foundation: The Chaldean, or Neo-Babylonian, Empire did not grow by gradual expansion; it took advantage of the collapse of another empire. Nabopolassar, a leader of uncertain origin traditionally regarded as a Chaldean chieftain, seized Babylon in 626 BCE amid the turmoil that followed the death of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. The coronation of Nabopolassar, in late November of that year, restored native Babylonian kingship after more than a century of Assyrian domination. The early state was fragile; several southern Mesopotamian cities passed back and forth between Babylonian and Assyrian control for nearly a decade. The turning point was the alliance with Cyaxares of Media, which produced the sack of Nineveh in 612 BCE and, after the fall of Harran in 610–609 BCE, the destruction of Assyrian power. The Battle of Carchemish in 605 BCE, won by the crown prince Nebuchadnezzar II against the Egyptian army of Pharaoh Necho II, secured the Levant and turned a regional kingdom into the dominant power of the ancient Near East. Nabopolassar died shortly afterwards, and Nebuchadnezzar hurried back to Babylon to take the throne. He reigned for forty-three years.
fields.socioeconomy: Babylon under the Chaldeans was among the largest and wealthiest cities in the ancient world, the commercial and ceremonial centre of Mesopotamian civilisation. Its agriculture depended on the ancient irrigation networks of the Tigris-Euphrates valley, maintained and extended under Nebuchadnezzar through heavy state investment in canals. Trade networks reached from the Persian Gulf to the Levantine coast, and Babylon was an entrepôt for goods moving between Egypt, Arabia, Anatolia and the Iranian plateau. The deportation policy, most famously applied to Judah in 597 and 587/586 BCE, had an economic as well as a political purpose: craftsmen, administrators and labourers were resettled in Babylonia to supply the enormous building programmes under way there. The Ishtar Gate, the Processional Way, the rebuilt temple of Marduk with its ziggurat Etemenanki, the South Palace and the Hanging Gardens, whose existence is still debated, all show a state putting surplus revenue into monumental architecture with deliberate ideological intent. The population was ethnically diverse. It included Babylonians, Chaldean tribal groups, tribal Aramaeans, deported peoples and a substantial business class, such as the Egibi family of Babylon, whose commercial records survive on thousands of cuneiform tablets.
fields.military: The Chaldean army was built on Assyrian military practice, adapted to a different strategy. Assyria had been an empire of continuous expansion. Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar operated mainly through annual campaigns in the west, siege warfare and the enforcement of vassalage, rather than through a dense network of garrisoned provinces. The capture of Jerusalem in 597 BCE, which led to the deportation of King Jehoiachin and the Judean elite, and the destruction of the city and its Temple after a second siege in 587/586 BCE, showed that the army could sustain operations far from home. The thirteen-year siege of the island city of Tyre, begun around 585 BCE, showed the empire's strategic ambition and also the limits of its siege capability against a maritime target: it ended in a negotiated submission rather than a sack. The failed invasion of Egypt in 601 BCE, in which both armies suffered heavy losses according to the Babylonian Chronicle, was the one significant military reversal of Nebuchadnezzar's reign and temporarily shook the loyalty of his Levantine vassals. After Nebuchadnezzar's death the army remained intact but was never again led by a commander of comparable ability.
fields.governance: The Chaldean state governed Mesopotamia and the Levant through direct administration in the Babylonian heartland and vassal arrangements in outlying territories. Nebuchadnezzar upheld the ancient Babylonian tradition of royal legitimacy through religious duty, performing the New Year (Akitu) festival rites that affirmed his relationship with the god Marduk and his temple, the Esagila. Political legitimacy rested on this bond between crown and priesthood. Provincial governors administered outlying territories, while deported populations were settled in organised communities with their own internal leadership, as among the Judean exiles by the Chebar canal near Nippur. The legal tradition drew on centuries of Mesopotamian jurisprudence, though no comprehensive Chaldean law code comparable to Hammurabi's survives. The system proved fragile after 562 BCE, when the absence of a strong successor showed that authority had been concentrated in Nebuchadnezzar's person rather than distributed across durable administrative structures.
fields.impact: The Chaldean Empire's lasting effects were cultural and religious rather than political. The destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BCE and the Babylonian captivity changed the development of Judaism, accelerating the shift from a temple-centred, territorially rooted religion to a portable, text-centred faith capable of surviving in exile. This change had far-reaching consequences for Christianity and Islam. Babylonian astronomy and mathematics flourished in this period. Systematic records of celestial phenomena such as the Astronomical Diaries later informed Hellenistic astronomy, so much so that “Chaldean” became a byword for astronomer and astrologer in the Greek and Roman worlds. The city of Babylon itself became the archetype of imperial grandeur across many traditions, featuring in Hebrew scripture, Greek historiography and later Christian apocalyptic literature. Trade connections maintained under Nebuchadnezzar kept Mesopotamia integrated into the wider Near Eastern commercial network linking the Mediterranean to the Iranian plateau and Arabia.
fields.decline: The collapse of the Chaldean Empire was out of proportion to its former power and was driven largely by internal failure rather than by any long military decline. Four kings, Amel-Marduk, Neriglissar, Labashi-Marduk and Nabonidus, took the throne in the six years after Nebuchadnezzar's death in 562 BCE, and most of the successions involved assassination or coup. The last king, Nabonidus, lacked dynastic legitimacy and added religious alienation to it: he favoured the moon god Sin over Marduk and spent roughly a decade at the Arabian oasis of Tayma while his son Belshazzar governed in Babylon. The Nabonidus Chronicle records year after year in which the New Year festival, which required the king's presence, was not held. When Cyrus the Great's Persian forces defeated the Babylonian army at Opis in the autumn of 539 BCE, Babylon itself fell without meaningful resistance in October; the Marduk priesthood appears to have welcomed Cyrus, and the Cyrus Cylinder presented the conquest as a divinely ordained restoration.
fields.summary: The Chaldean Empire lasted 87 years and was perhaps the most consequential state of that length in ancient history: its cultural and religious effects outlasted by millennia every political structure that succeeded it.
fields.teaser: The Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem, raised the Ishtar Gate and made Babylon one of antiquity's greatest cities. It is credited with the legendary Hanging Gardens, whose existence is still debated.
fields.t0: The Neo-Babylonian Empire rose on Assyria's ruins and, under Nebuchadnezzar II, dominated the Near East.
fields.t1: Its destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian captivity reshaped Judaism into a portable, text-centred faith.
fields.t2: Weak successors and a king who neglected Marduk let Cyrus the Great take Babylon almost unopposed in 539 BCE.
fields.dyk: Babylonian sky-watching was so well known that 'Chaldean' became a byword for astronomer and astrologer in the Greek and Roman worlds.
